pin.khoa: Four days later, the French and Spanish fleets gathered in the bay: forty-seven ships of the line by the British count, fifty by the Spanish. The Duc de Crillon led the siege. Their answer to red-hot shot: ten floating batteries, designed by the French engineer d'Arçon. A French account says he'd asked to test them against red-hot shot first. It was refused. The thirteenth of September 1782. That morning, the batteries moved into position under the garrison's fire. At ten twenty-five, by the Spanish account, the attackers' guns, some four hundred, opened fire together. By the next afternoon, all ten batteries were lost. Over two thousand attackers were lost, by a British estimate that includes prisoners, and by a Spanish one; the British rescued three hundred and fifty-seven.
